title: Ideal Gases and Thermal Properties
seo_title: SSS 2 Chemistry: Ideal Gases and Thermal Properties Worksheets (WAEC/NECO)
standard_code: SSS 2 Chemistry: Ideal Gases and Thermal Properties
standard_text: The kinetic theory of gases; the ideal gas; Boyle's law, Charles's law and the pressure–temperature law; the general gas equation p₁V₁/T₁ = p₂V₂/T₂; the ideal gas equation pV = nRT; temperature in kelvin. (summary of the senior secondary Chemistry curriculum, SSS 2; WAEC and NECO syllabuses)
meta_desc: Free SSS 2 Chemistry worksheets (senior secondary curriculum, WAEC and NECO): the kinetic molecular theory, boyle's and Charles's laws, the combined and ideal gas laws, gas laws and the ideal gas equation. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Always use the temperature in kelvin: T = θ + 273.
body_html:
How to think about it

The kinetic theory: a gas is made of particles in random motion; pressure is caused by collisions with the container walls; the average kinetic energy is proportional to the kelvin temperature. An ideal gas has particles with no volume and no forces between them.

Boyle's law: pV is constant at constant temperature. Charles's law: V/T is constant at constant pressure. For a fixed mass of gas p₁V₁/T₁ = p₂V₂/T₂. The ideal gas equation is pV = nRT, with R = 8.31 J·K⁻¹·mol⁻¹, p in Pa and V in m³.

Example

A gas at 300 K and 2 dm³ is heated to 600 K at constant pressure. New volume?

V/T is constant

Answer: 4 dm³

Example

Convert 27 °C to kelvin.

+273

Answer: 300 K

Common mistakes

  • Using °C in gas law calculations.
  • Using dm³ in pV = nRT without changing to m³.
  • Thinking gas particles stop at 0 °C.

faq.q: When do real gases behave least like ideal gases?
faq.a: At high pressure and low temperature, when the particles are close together and attract each other.

faq.q: Why does a tyre's pressure increase on a hot day?
faq.a: The particles move faster and hit the walls more often and harder.

items.q: A sealed can of gas is heated. Why does the pressure increase?
c: The mass of each particle changes.
The particles move faster, so they hit the walls more often and with more force.
The particles hit each other more often, not the walls.
items.e: Gas pressure comes from particles colliding with the walls of the container.

items.q: Which state of matter is described? “Particles are closely packed in a regular pattern.”
items.e: Solid: close, regular, vibrate. Liquid: close, random, slide past each other. Gas: far apart, random, fast.

items.q: Why does a metal rod expand when it is heated?
c: The particles vibrate more and move slightly further apart.
items.e: The kinetic particle model: all matter is made of tiny particles in constant random motion.

items.q: Calculate the mean kinetic energy of a gas molecule at 5,800 K.

items.e: Solid: close, regular, vibrate. Liquid: close, random, slide past each other. Gas: far apart, random, fast.

Which state of matter is described? “Particles are closely packed but in a random arrangement.”
items.e: Solid: close, regular, vibrate. Liquid: close, random, slide past each other. Gas: far apart, random, fast.

items.q: Why is a liquid hard to compress?
c: Its particles are already close together.
It has strong forces like a solid in a regular pattern.
items.e: The kinetic particle model: all matter is made of tiny particles in constant random motion.

items.q: A sealed balloon of air is left in the hot sun. What happens to the pressure of the gas?
items.e: The particles gain kinetic energy and hit the walls harder and more often, and the balloon expands.

items.e: Gas pressure comes from particles colliding with the walls of the container.

items.e: Solid: close, regular, vibrate. Liquid: close, random, slide past each other. Gas: far apart, random, fast.

items.e: The kinetic particle model: all matter is made of tiny particles in constant random motion.
